issues.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires an interest in land after an acquisition notification cannot challenge the acquisition and may only claim compensation.
material_facts: The land was notified for acquisition before the society entered into an agreement to sell with the original landholders.
The agreement to sell did not transfer title to the society, and the original landholders did not join the society's later petition.
issues.conclusion: The society could not challenge the acquisition as a subsequent transferee; a transferee in that position may only claim compensation.
issues.legal_principle: A transfer made after an acquisition notification is void as against the Government and does not bind it; a subsequent purchaser cannot challenge the acquisition and may claim compensation. The Court relied on Gian Chand v. Gopala, Yadu Nandan Garg v. State of Rajasthan, Jaipur Development Authority v. Mahavir Housing Cooperative Society, Secretary, Jaipur Development Authority v. Daulat Mal Jain, Meera Sahni v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi, Har Narain v. Mam Chand, and V. Chandrasekaran v. The Administrative Officer. It also relied on Smt. Kalawati v. Bisheshwar and State of Kerala v. M.K. Kunhikannan Nambiar for the meaning of “void.”

predicates.acquisition_challenge_by_transferee: A transferee brings a proceeding challenging the acquisition of the land in which the transferee claims an interest.
predicates.transfer_after_acquisition_notice: The landowner transfers or agrees to transfer an interest in the land after the acquisition notice has been issued.

issues.definition: When a transferee challenges an acquisition after acquiring an interest in the land following the acquisition notice, the transferee cannot challenge the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A prior final determination of an acquisition challenge confines a later proceeding to any expressly permitted ground for relief.
material_facts: The society and original landholders previously challenged the acquisition, and the challenge was dismissed for delay and upheld on further challenge.
The prior order permitted a later proceeding on the ground of discriminatory treatment in releasing other land.
The society's later proceeding sought release of its land, relying on alleged discrimination.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition challenge had attained finality, and the society could pursue only the permitted claim based on discrimination; the acquisition itself could not be reopened.
issues.legal_principle: Acquisition proceedings cannot be challenged at a belated stage once the challenge has been dismissed and the determination has attained finality. The Court treated the liberty granted in the earlier proceeding as limited to a claim of discrimination in the release of land.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: A proceeding seeks to challenge the validity of an acquisition.
predicates.prior_challenge_final: An earlier challenge to the same acquisition has been dismissed and that determination has become final.
predicates.renewed_ground_outside_permitted_scope: The later challenge relies on a ground not allowed by the limited permission given in the earlier proceeding.

issues.definition: A later acquisition challenge is barred when an earlier challenge is final and the later ground falls outside the scope permitted for a subsequent proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to equal treatment in the release of acquired land requires proof of an enforceable right and genuinely comparable cases, and cannot rest on unlawful benefits granted to others.
material_facts: The society claimed that other land had been released while its land remained acquired.
The other releases concerned land released for different reasons, including land acquired for another public purpose, land with existing construction, or land without access.
The society did not establish that the other beneficiaries were similarly situated, including that they also lacked title and had acquired their claimed interest after the acquisition notice.
The society's telegram alleging discrimination did not set out a factual foundation or identify comparable cases.
issues.conclusion: The society did not establish discrimination or a right to release by parity, and Article 14 could not be used to perpetuate an unlawful release of land.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 applies to invidious discrimination between equals or similarly circumstanced persons without a rational basis; it does not provide negative equality or perpetuate illegality. A party alleging discrimination must plead the factual foundation and details of comparable cases. The Court relied on Smt. Sneh Prabha v. State of U.P., Yogesh Kumar v. Government of NCT Delhi, State of West Bengal v. Debasish Mukherjee, Priya Gupta v. State of Chhattisgarh, Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Madhu Kishwar v. State of Bihar, Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra, M/s Video Electronics v. State of Punjab, Vishundas Hundumal v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and Eskayef Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise.

rule.if: discrimination_claim and (not comparable_cases_established or not independent_enforceable_right or comparator_benefit_unlawful)

predicates.discrimination_claim: A claimant seeks the same treatment as other persons whose land was released from acquisition.
predicates.comparable_cases_established: The claimant pleads and establishes facts showing that the other beneficiaries were similarly situated in the relevant respects.
predicates.independent_enforceable_right: The claimant establishes an independent legal right to the relief sought.
predicates.comparator_benefit_unlawful: The benefit received by the proposed comparators was contrary to law.

issues.definition: A claim for parity-based release is unavailable when the claimant has not established comparable cases or an independent enforceable right, or when the comparison relies on an unlawful benefit.

issues.legal_issue: A writ of mandamus cannot be used to create a right or to have a court substitute its decision for that of the competent statutory authority.
material_facts: The society did not apply to the authority responsible for the acquisition seeking release of the land.

The society had applied to other authorities for scheme approval and conversion of land use, and later sent a telegram to the Chief Secretary alleging injustice without adequate details of the discrimination claimed.
The High Court ordered the land released rather than leaving any statutory question of release to the competent authority.
issues.conclusion: The society had not established a basis for the High Court to order release, and the High Court could not itself take over the task of the statutory authority.
issues.legal_principle: A writ exists to enforce an established legal right and corresponding duty, not to create a right. A mandamus ordinarily requires a clear demand to an authority with power to act and a refusal of that demand, unless demand is manifestly futile or an empty formality. If a matter has been placed before the appropriate authority and remains undecided, the court may direct that authority to decide it by a reasoned order, but should not decide the matter itself. The Court relied on Commissioner of Police, Bombay v. Govardhandas Bhanji, Praga Tools Corporation v. C.V. Imanual, Punjab Financial Corporation v. Garg Steel, Union of India v. Arulmozhi Iniarasu, Khela Banerjee v. City Montessori School, G. Veerappa Pillai v. Raman and Raman, Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Asha Ramchandra Ambedkar, H.P. Public Service Commission v. Mukesh Thakur, and Manohar Lal v. Ugrasen.

rule.if: writ_seeking_mandamus and (not established_legal_right_or_duty or (not clear_demand_to_competent_authority and demand_not_excused) or not authority_refused_demand)

predicates.writ_seeking_mandamus: A proceeding asks a court to compel a public authority to perform an act.
predicates.established_legal_right_or_duty: The applicant establishes an existing legal right or a corresponding duty of the authority.
predicates.clear_demand_to_competent_authority: The applicant makes a clear demand to an authority empowered to perform the requested act.
predicates.demand_not_excused: The facts do not make a demand unnecessary because it would be futile or an empty formality.
predicates.authority_refused_demand: The competent authority has rejected the demand, by words or conduct.

issues.definition: Mandamus should not issue when the applicant has no established right or corresponding duty, or when a necessary clear demand to the competent authority has not been made and refused.

issues.legal_issue: Acquired land that has vested in the State after possession is taken cannot be released from acquisition by later divesting the State of its title.
material_facts: The Government took possession of the acquired land and handed it over to the acquiring corporation.
The society sought release of land after possession had been taken and the land had vested in the State free from encumbrances.
issues.conclusion: The land could not be released after possession had been taken and it had vested in the State.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, permits withdrawal from acquisition only before possession is taken; once the land vests in the State free from encumbrances, it cannot be divested. The Court relied on this principle in considering the Government circular and the request for release.

predicates.acquired_land_release_claim: A claimant asks a public authority or court to release land from an acquisition.
predicates.possession_taken_and_land_vested: The State has taken possession of the acquired land and the land has vested in it free from encumbrances.

issues.definition: A release claim cannot succeed when possession of the acquired land has been taken and the land has vested in the State.

issues.legal_issue: Executive instructions cannot override statutory law, and a public authority cannot be estopped from complying with the law.
material_facts: Government circulars provided for exemptions or regularisation in circumstances that included later purchasers and agreements to sell made after an acquisition notice.
The society relied on those circulars to seek release of land despite the post-notice agreement and the completed acquisition.
The circulars were inconsistent with the law governing acquisition and release of acquired land.
issues.conclusion: The society could not obtain release by relying on the inconsistent circulars, and the State was not bound by an erroneous prior understanding or action contrary to law.
issues.legal_principle: Executive instructions without statutory force cannot override statutory law, and there can be no estoppel against law or public policy; a statutory authority cannot be compelled to act beyond its powers or contrary to its duty. The Court relied on B.N. Nagarajan v. State of Mysore, Sant Ram Sharma v. State of Rajasthan, Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Umadevi, Mahadeo Bhau Khilare v. State of Maharashtra, State of Madras v. K.M. Rajagopalan, Badri Prasad v. Nagarmal, Dr. H.S. Rikhy v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, Surajmull Nagoremull v. Triton Insurance, and Shiba Prasad Singh v. Srish Chandra Nandi.

predicates.public_authority_land_dispute: A claimant seeks relief from a public authority concerning land subject to a statutory acquisition.
predicates.executive_instruction_conflicts_with_law: An executive instruction purports to permit an outcome inconsistent with the governing law.

issues.definition: In a public-authority land dispute, an executive instruction inconsistent with the law cannot support the relief sought.

issues.legal_issue: Land acquired for one public purpose is not justified for release when the claimant seeks to use it for a purpose incompatible with the acquisition scheme.
material_facts: The land was acquired for industrial development.
The society sought the land to develop residential housing.
The society did not show that the proposed residential use was compatible with the industrial development scheme.
issues.conclusion: The society's request to use the acquired land for residential development was not justified.
issues.legal_principle: Land may be released where its existing use is the same as the purpose for which it was acquired and its retention would not hinder development, subject to the relevant scheme and circumstances. The Court found that residential development was inconsistent with the industrial purpose here. It relied on Union of India v. Bal Ram Singh, Sube Singh v. State of Haryana, Jagdish Chand v. State of Haryana, and Dharam Pal v. State of Haryana.

predicates.acquired_land_release_claim: A claimant seeks release of land that has been acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.proposed_use_incompatible_with_acquisiti: The claimant proposes to use the land for a purpose incompatible with the purpose and development scheme for which it was acquired.

issues.definition: A release claim is not justified when the proposed use of acquired land is incompatible with the acquisition purpose.
